newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Summit NZ, Aust tests significant.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Summit NZ, Aust tests significant.

text.p: Within the space of a week, market minnow Summit Gold NL has announced two of the most significant mining test results since listing in 1987, rocketing it from relative obscurity into the investor limelight.
Summit on Friday said drilling results from its Valhalla project in northwest Queensland had revealed wide zones of uranium mineralisation.
On Tuesday, the company said it had received encouraging results from its gold prospect at Carrick in Central Otago.
"That's how it happens. All your good luck comes at once," Managing Director Alan Eggers told Reuters from Perth.
But he said it was too early to say in both cases how far away the company was from production in either case, if at all.
"But I would think these developments would be the most significant since the company listed," Eggers said.
Summit, "junior explorer", has never made a profit.
"This is extremely good news because we have not drilled a very large part of the known extent of this (Valhalla) deposit," Wellington-based Chairman Colin Beyer said.
"We are still trying to determine the size and nature of the deposit, but it's looking very good."
In Otago the surface indications were also positive.
Summit's share price spiked up sharply on Friday to a peak of NZ$0.85 against a year low of 7.3 cents, before settling back to a close of $0.60, up 22 cents.

"The share price gain was not unexpected from our point of view, because the Valhalla thing is a very significant discovery by world standards," Beyer said. "Most of the Mount Isa mineral occurrences get better at depth, and it looks as if it's showing that type of scenario."
Valhalla had been drilled by Queensland Mines Ltd in the 1960s and 70s, identifying a resource of about 10 million tonnes at around two pounds of uranium oxide per tonne.
"Queensland Mines believed Valhalla did not have much further potential and metallurgically it was quite difficult to treat, and so that's where it sat," Eggers said.
Summit's deep diamond drilling programme confirmed the resource was there but that it was much larger, with an improved grade of 4.92 pounds.
"All three deep holes hit good widths of mineralisation so it's open going down in depth. We have not found the bottom of the deposit," Eggers said.
"The potential is for a much larger deposit than we have announced, which puts it into a class of a very significant deposit in terms of size," he said.
Valhalla would rate as Australia's third or fourth largest undeveloped uranium deposit as it stands and at a grade of 4.92 it was sufficent to be commercial, if it can be recovered.
Because of the potential size of the deposit, economies of scale meant a lot could be done with it. Testing would establish how much could be extracted and at what cost.
Summit is about 33-34 percent owned by directors since a management buyout early this year, and Eggers is the largest holder with 10-12 percent.
Valhalla lies on a pastoral lease and the site is not subject to hay native land claim, he said.
Summit is the operator for Valhalla and Resolute Ltd is the other 50 percent partner.

Commenting on Otago, Eggers said the two kilometre-long arsenic gold anomaly was similar in structure to the nearby Macraes Mining in North Otago. Macraes' former chief geologist Geoff Price is now consulting and running the Carrick project.
Eggers expected Carrick to yield low grade ore, like Macraes, of something like 1.5-2.0 grammes per tonne.
Summit is a New Zealand corportion, listed in New Zealand and Australia. -- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
